openers.adaptation-and-resilience: Cutting emissions limits how much the climate changes, but some change is already locked in. The oceans are rising, and faster than before, as warmer seawater expands and land ice melts. This chapter is about living with that: adjusting to climate change, coping with its floods and droughts, and bouncing back afterward. It asks what makes some people more open to harm than others, what adapting costs, who pays for it, and why private investors hold back. It ends where adaptation runs out, at the limits beyond which no adjustment can protect people or ecosystems.

reviews.adaptation-and-resilience: Climate risk comes from three ingredients together: a hazard, the people and assets exposed to it, and their vulnerability. Adaptation works on the last two, through seawalls and retreat, early warning, insurance, new planting times and protected mangroves. Yet the money falls far short: developing countries need 10–18 times the international public adaptation finance they receive, and private investors shy away because adaptation rarely earns a clear income. Poorly chosen measures can even backfire as maladaptation. Where adaptation reaches its limits, what remains is loss and damage, and the fight over who should pay for it is still unresolved.

nature-clim-002.title: Climate change adaptation: learning to live with a warmer world
nature-clim-002.text: A seawall, a new insurance scheme, a farmer sowing a few weeks earlier, a green roof on a city block. Each is a form of adaptation, the process of adjusting to the current and expected effects of {{ref:nature-hist-007}}. The goal is to reduce harm and to take advantage of any opportunities the change brings. Adaptation usually goes alongside mitigation, which limits warming by cutting greenhouse gas emissions. One deals with the causes, the other with the {{ref:nature-eco-017}}. Adaptation can be reactive, responding to impacts after they arrive. It can also be proactive, preparing for change before it comes. It matters most in developing countries, which are the most vulnerable to climate change. The idea took a while to win respect. In the early 1990s many saw adaptation as a distraction from mitigation. It gained attention only in 2009–2010, after the Copenhagen Summit. Today more than 70% of countries have adaptation plans, but actual implementation is limited and uneven. Knowledge gaps, behavioural resistance and market failures all slow it down, which is why policy is needed. Politics adds a deeper problem. Politicians are rewarded for short-term change, so long-term adaptation is hard to carry through.

nature-clim-037.title: Sea level rise: the ocean that keeps climbing
nature-clim-037.text: Between 1901 and 2018 the world's average sea level rose 15–25 cm, faster than in at least 3,000 years. Sea level rise is this climb in average ocean level, and it has sped up sharply. By 2013–2022 the rate had reached 4.62 mm per year. Two causes dominate. From 1993 to 2018, melting ice sheets and glaciers caused 44% of the rise, the process described in {{ref:nature-eco-021}}. Thermal expansion, water swelling as it warms, caused another 42%. The sea responds slowly. It lags temperature by decades, so it will keep accelerating to 2050 from warming already caused. What happens after that depends on emissions. By 2100 the sea could stand 30 cm to 1.0 m above the early 2020s with very deep emission cuts, or up to 1.9 m with high emissions. The damage takes many forms: more storm-surge flooding, coastal erosion, lost mangroves, saltier irrigation water and damaged ports. Low-lying Caribbean and Pacific islands face the greatest near-term impact, and many may become uninhabitable this century. Socially and economically vulnerable communities are often more exposed and have fewer resources to adapt.

nature-clim-014.title: Climate resilience: coping, recovering and learning
nature-clim-014.text: When a flood or drought strikes, some communities recover and others do not. Climate resilience is how well people or ecosystems can cope with, and bounce back from, such hazards. The IPCC defines it as the capacity of social, economic and ecosystems to cope with a hazardous event, trend or disturbance, including the ability to reorganise and learn. The definition is heavily debated, in concept and in practice, because the idea crosses many disciplines. One framework splits it into three capacities: adaptive, anticipatory and absorptive. Resilience differs from {{ref:nature-clim-002}}, which is any adjustment to climate impacts; resilience is a more systematic way of absorbing change and reorganising. Most resilience work so far maintains existing systems, such as seawalls protecting a coastal town. That is an incremental approach, not a transformational one. Long-lived infrastructure needs risk-based engineering and economic analysis to be designed for resilience under uncertain projections.

nature-clim-025.title: Vulnerability: what makes some places easy to hurt
nature-clim-025.text: The same storm can wreck one town and spare another. Vulnerability is the state of being open to harm; for hazards, it means the features of a community, system or asset that make it susceptible to damage. In disasters, vulnerability ties people's relationship with their environment to social forces, institutions and cultural values. It is not just about the weather. Risk rises with it: the more vulnerable a community, the more risk it faces. Indicators of vulnerability cover external shocks and stresses as well as an internal inability to cope. Climate vulnerability is generally a bigger problem in low-income countries than in high-income ones.

nature-clim-001.title: Adaptive capacity: the stock of ways to adjust
nature-clim-001.text: Adaptive capacity is the ability of people, institutions, ecosystems and other organisms to adjust to potential harm, seize opportunities or cope with consequences. In climate risk it sits alongside hazard, exposure and {{ref:nature-clim-025}} as a key ingredient. It works like a stock of resources and assets, drawn on as future conditions require. In societies it rests on institutions that learn, flexible decision-making and power structures that respond to everyone with a stake. The ODI's local adaptive capacity framework names five features: assets, institutions and entitlements, knowledge, innovation, and flexible forward-looking governance. A stable, prosperous economy helps, and wealthier nations are generally better prepared. Barriers to adaptation can be overcome, whereas limits cannot. A common external barrier is a lack of land to relocate to. For species, adaptive capacity depends on phenotypic plasticity, the ability to change form or behavior, on dispersal ability and on genetic diversity.

nature-clim-004.title: The adaptation gap: a bill far bigger than the budget
nature-clim-004.text: Adapting to climate change is expensive, and the price rises sharply with each extra step of warming. Globally the cost likely runs to tens or hundreds of billions of dollars a year for decades. The IPCC puts it at $15 to 411 billion per year to 2030, with most estimates above $100 billion. The adaptation gap is the shortfall between that cost and the money available. UNEP's 2023 report put the gap in funding at $194 billion to $366 billion a year. Developing countries' needs, $215 to $387 billion a year, are 10–18 times current international public money for adaptation. The gap is widening because most tracked money for climate action goes to {{ref:nature-clim-149}} instead. The spending would often pay off. In many specific settings, adaptation costs less than the damage it avoids, though global estimates are very uncertain.

nature-clim-009.title: Why private money avoids adaptation
nature-clim-009.text: A solar farm sells electricity. A flood barrier sells nothing. That contrast explains why private investors find adaptation harder to fund than {{ref:nature-clim-149}}: adaptation usually lacks a clear income stream. It often serves non-market sectors or public goods that benefit many people at once, so few projects attract private money. Timing works against it too. The costs come now while the benefits come later, and investors prefer short-term returns. Uncertainty about future impacts and benefits leaves them short of information. Still, innovation is increasing the potential for private finance to help close the adaptation gap.

nature-clim-012.title: Hazard, exposure and vulnerability: the three parts of climate risk
nature-clim-012.text: A storm is only part of the story. Climate risk needs three ingredients together: the hazard, the exposure of people and assets, and their vulnerability. Exposure is the presence of people, livelihoods, ecosystems and assets in places that could be harmed. It falls when people retreat from floodplains. Better early warning and evacuation also reduce it. {{ref:nature-clim-025}}, in the IPCC's words a propensity to be adversely affected, includes sensitivity and a lack of capacity to cope. Insurance, more varied livelihoods, social protection and sturdier infrastructure all reduce it. So does nature. Protecting mangroves, which dampen storm energy, is ecosystem-based adaptation that cuts vulnerability.

nature-clim-027.title: Climate change vulnerability: who stands to be hurt most
nature-clim-027.text: About 3.3 to 3.6 billion people were estimated in 2021 to live in highly vulnerable contexts. Climate change vulnerability is how strongly people or ecosystems are likely to be harmed by climate change; formally, their propensity to be adversely affected. It includes their capacity to cope and adapt, and it is one component of climate risk. The definition has shifted. Earlier IPCC reports made vulnerability a function of exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity; the Fifth report moved exposure out as a separate element of risk. People with low incomes, {{ref:nature-gov-184}}, women, children and the elderly tend to be more vulnerable. Developing countries were judged more vulnerable, partly because adaptation costs are high relative to their GDP, the total value of what an economy produces. Vulnerability can be reduced by adaptation, by tackling poverty, inequality and conflict, and by mitigation that makes impacts less severe.

nature-clim-226.title: Disaster risk reduction: acting before the disaster
nature-clim-226.text: After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, 77% of the deaths in North Aceh were female. Disasters do not strike everyone equally, and women and girls are disproportionately harmed. Disaster risk reduction, or DRR, tries to change the odds beforehand. It covers actions that make disasters less likely and less damaging, by preventing new risk, reducing existing risk and managing what remains. Disaster risk is the potential loss of life, injury or damaged assets, arising from hazard, vulnerability and exposure together, the {{ref:nature-clim-012}}. DRR aims to make communities stronger and better prepared: more resilient and less vulnerable. Its scope is much broader than conventional emergency management. Disaster risk management, a name sometimes used for the whole field, is its practical implementation. Since the mid-1970s the field has shifted from response and recovery toward understanding causes and reducing risk in advance. Experts often see climate change adaptation as one of many processes within it.

nature-clim-005.title: International adaptation finance: helping poorer countries adapt
nature-clim-005.text: In 2009 rich nations pledged $100 billion a year by 2020 for mitigation and adaptation in developing countries. By December 2020 that money had not been fully delivered. International adaptation finance is money from richer countries and international funds that helps developing countries adapt. Several UNFCCC funds serve this purpose: the Special Climate Change Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund and {{ref:nature-clim-031}}. {{ref:nature-clim-051}}, created in 2010, is another channel. Adaptation still gets the smaller share. It received only 21% of public climate money provided in 2020. Multilateral development banks gave over €19 billion for adaptation in 2021. In 2022 nations agreed to set up a fund for harms beyond what adaptation can handle.

nature-clim-008.title: Limits to adaptation: where adjusting stops working
nature-clim-008.text: Adaptation cannot protect against everything. Its limits are the points beyond which it can no longer shield people or ecosystems from climate risks. The IPCC's 2022 report separates soft limits, where options exist but are not yet usable, from hard limits, where none remain. Some systems in Australia, small islands, the Americas, Africa and Europe have already hit soft limits. At 1.5 °C, glacier-dependent regions and small islands reach hard limits. At 2 °C many staple crops hit soft limits. As risks grow, small incremental adjustments stop being enough. Larger and costlier transformational adaptation becomes necessary.

nature-clim-018.title: Loss and damage: the harms nobody prevented
nature-clim-018.text: Some climate harms get through every defense. Loss and damage names those harms, the ones mitigation and adaptation fail to prevent, and the question of how to deal with them. Loss means irreversible harm, such as an extinct species or an island lost to the sea. Damage means harm that can be repaired or compensated. Economic losses affect traded goods and services. Non-economic losses, such as lost family members or cultures, involve things no market trades. The idea covers sudden disasters like cyclones and slow change like sea level rise. The IPCC found such residual risks will rise with further warming. How to respond is disputed. Small island and least developed countries have long sought liability and compensation, which developed countries resist. In 1991 small island states proposed an insurance pool funded by countries' shares of emissions and income; it was rejected. A 2026 study estimated that US CO2 emissions from 1990 to 2020 had caused $10.2 trillion in cumulative damages by 2020.

nature-nbs-081.title: Maladaptation: when adapting makes things worse
nature-nbs-081.text: An air conditioner cools a hot room, but if it runs on carbon-intensive electricity it adds to the emissions behind the heat. That is maladaptation: an adaptation action that ends up increasing vulnerability or reducing the ability to adapt sustainably later. The IPCC introduced the term in 2001. It describes actions that may raise climate-related risk through higher emissions, shifted vulnerability, more unequal outcomes or reduced welfare. The harm is usually unintended. Seawalls can waterlog fields and reduce soil fertility. Adapting to short-term climate swings can also clash with longer trends, as when irrigation was expanded into Egypt's Western Sinai desert despite projected drying. Community-driven, bottom-up approaches generally carry a lower risk of maladaptation than top-down technical fixes.

nature-clim-038.title: Retreat, accommodate or protect: adapting to rising seas
nature-clim-038.text: Cutting emissions can slow {{ref:nature-clim-037}} after 2050 but cannot stop it, so adaptation is inevitable. Societies have three broad choices: retreat, accommodate coastal change, or protect coasts with defences. Hard adaptation relies on capital-intensive infrastructure such as seawalls. Soft adaptation strengthens natural defences like dunes, using local, modular means. The economics can be striking. Without adaptation, annual flood costs in 136 large coastal cities could reach $1 trillion by 2050. Adaptation costing $50 billion per year could cut that to a little over $60 billion. But protection is not shared evenly. Higher-value areas are more likely to be defended, leaving lower-value areas to retreat. Retreat often costs people their livelihoods, and displaced people can strain their new communities. Planning lags too: in a 2023 survey, 98% of planners knew the projections, but 26% had not yet put them into policy.

nature-clim-225.title: Climate risk insurance: fast money after the storm
nature-clim-225.text: Climate risk insurance is designed to cover the financial risks of climate change, especially {{ref:nature-eco-001}}. Its appeal is speed. It provides money quickly after a disaster for relief and rebuilding, and helps prepare to reduce future vulnerability. It is often seen as a way to make poor and developing communities more resilient, and as an important adaptation measure. Its scale is a challenge. Insurance works by pooling many separate risks, but weather disasters hit whole regions at once and trigger many claims together. Because climate risks are partly correlated in this way, pooling works less well, so cover must be sold at a large, diversified scale. High premiums in risky areas could discourage people from settling there. The InsuResilience Global Partnership, launched at COP23, supports such schemes. Opinion is split. Supporters see a safety net, while critics say it puts the cost on communities that emitted least, and start-up and data costs are high for low-income countries.

nature-clim-034.title: Early warning systems: buying time before a hazard hits
nature-clim-034.text: Interest in early warning surged after the Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004. An early warning system is a chain of sensors, detection and communication that spots hazards early and gives people time to prepare and limit harm. A complete system has four parts: risk analysis, monitoring and warning, spreading the message, and the capability to respond. Technology alone is not enough. To work, a system must involve at-risk communities, raise awareness, deliver alerts effectively and keep people prepared. The UN recommends early warning systems as key to climate adaptation. It runs the Climate Risk and Early Warning Systems partnership for high-risk countries.

nature-clim-031.title: The Adaptation Fund: paying for adaptation through carbon credits
nature-clim-031.text: The Adaptation Fund pays for projects that help developing countries adapt, under {{ref:nature-clim-056}}. It was established in 2001 at COP7 in Marrakech and officially launched in 2007. Its original income was unusual: a 2% share of the credits issued for {{ref:nature-mkt-104}} projects. As carbon prices fell, donations from rich countries became more important. Its direct access mechanism lets accredited national and regional bodies in developing countries receive money directly. By 2024 it had committed over 1 billion US dollars since 2010 and reported over 43 million beneficiaries.

nature-clim-010.title: When adapting and cutting emissions help or hinder each other
nature-clim-010.text: Actions to adapt to climate change and actions to limit it can reinforce each other or work against each other. Public transport is a synergy. It produces lower emissions per kilometre and makes evacuation easier in disasters. Compact cities show the trade-off. They cut transport and building emissions, but packing buildings close together can worsen the urban heat island, the extra warmth that builds up in cities.

nature-clim-006.title: Additionality: new money or relabelled aid
nature-clim-006.text: Additionality is the principle that adaptation money should be extra to existing development aid, not redirected from it. Four main definitions exist. They range from finance additional to the Millennium Development Goals to climate money unconnected to aid budgets. The difference matters. Denmark raised adaptation aid from 0.09% to 0.12% of GDP between 2010 and 2020 by taking it from other aid. Critics also say the principle encourages business as usual, because it ignores future climate risks.

nature-clim-013.title: Climate services: climate information people can use
nature-clim-013.text: A forecast is only useful if someone can act on it. Climate services are systems that deliver usable climate information to people and organisations, to support decisions on adaptation, mitigation and risk. They help users foresee and manage the hazards of a changing climate. They are demand-driven. Instead of handing over research products, providers design them together with users, a process called co-design.

nature-clim-003.title: Four kinds of adaptation: built, institutional, behavioral and natural
nature-clim-003.text: Adaptation comes in four kinds. Infrastructural options use the built environment to protect against flooding, sea level rise and extreme heat. Institutional responses change the rules, through zoning, building codes, insurance schemes and coordination. Behavioural options change what people do, such as farmers shifting planting times or switching crops and livestock. Nature-based solutions work with ecosystems, aiming to benefit both people and biodiversity.

nature-clim-024.title: The economics of prevention: five to ten dollars saved per dollar
nature-clim-024.text: Every dollar spent on reducing disaster risk saves between $5 and $10 in disaster losses. The economics of {{ref:nature-clim-226}} looks at what disasters cost and makes the case for spending on prevention rather than only on response and recovery. The costs are large. Climate-related disasters cost over US$330 billion a year on average over 2015–2021, likely an underestimate. Yet the money flows the other way. Around 90% of international DRR funding goes to response and recovery, and only about 0.5% of development aid goes to reducing risk before disasters. For many countries, less than 1% of the national budget is available for DRR. New instruments are emerging, including rules requiring firms to disclose risk, resilience bonds and green bonds.

nature-clim-015.title: Climate resilient development: three goals pursued together
nature-clim-015.text: Climate resilient development pursues adaptation, mitigation and {{ref:nature-eecon-209}} together, using their synergies and reducing trade-offs, as described in {{ref:nature-clim-010}}. It has become a new paradigm for development, especially in the water sector, though the paradigm itself is contested. Governments on every continent are adopting policies for climate-resilient economies, pushed by {{ref:nature-clim-074}} and {{ref:nature-gov-010}}.

nature-clim-016.title: Measuring resilience with proxies
nature-clim-016.text: Money spent on resilience should go where it helps most. Resilience measurement provides tools and indicators for tracking the {{ref:nature-clim-014}} of households, communities or nations. It helps locate vulnerability hotspots and judge whether interventions work. The difficulty is that resilience has no single observable metric. It includes intangibles like social capital, the trust and networks people can draw on. So toolkits rely on long lists of proxy indicators, stand-ins that track it indirectly. Common objective measures include FAO's RIMA and the Livelihoods Change Over Time index.

nature-clim-032.title: Climate risk management: reducing harm and seizing gains
nature-clim-032.text: Climate risk management is a general approach to climate-sensitive decisions. It draws on adaptation, disaster management and development that can last to reduce vulnerability. Its tools include early response systems, diversification, flexible rules for allocating resources, insurance, infrastructure design and capacity building. It is not only defensive. It also seeks gains, such as farmers using a favourable seasonal forecast to raise their yields.

nature-clim-030.title: Ecological anthropology: how cultures fit their environments
nature-clim-030.text: Ecological anthropology is the branch of anthropology that studies how human cultures adapt to and shape their environments. It emerged in the 1960s from Julian Steward's cultural ecology. Roy Rappaport's work with the Maring of Papua New Guinea examined how ritual shaped the relationship between culture and nature. Critics said the field assumed static equilibrium and oversimplified systems, prompting a shift toward {{ref:nature-gov-227}}. Its practical legacy endures. Long-term {{ref:nature-gov-176}} can inform adaptation strategies and community monitoring.

nature-clim-023.title: The Sendai Framework: seven targets for safer societies
nature-clim-023.text: On March 18, 2015, countries adopted the Sendai Framework, an international plan setting seven targets for reducing disaster risk to 2030. Its targets aim to cut disaster deaths, the number of people affected, economic loss and damage to infrastructure. Others aim to widen access to warning systems, increase aid to developing countries and spread national DRR strategies. That last goal has made progress. Countries with national strategies rose from 55 to 123 by 2022.

nature-clim-093.title: The Loss and Damage Fund: a breakthrough after three decades
nature-clim-093.text: At COP27 in Egypt in 2022, countries agreed to create a fund for communities where adaptation is inadequate or comes too late. It came after three decades of negotiation on {{ref:nature-clim-018}}, and many saw it as a major breakthrough. It operates as a financial mechanism of {{ref:nature-clim-074}}. How to fill it remains open. Before the June 2023 Paris finance summit, over 100 economists proposed an extreme wealth tax to fund loss and damage; it was not adopted.

nature-clim-019.title: The Warsaw International Mechanism: talking about loss without liability
nature-clim-019.text: Created in 2013, the Warsaw International Mechanism is the UN body that addresses {{ref:nature-clim-018}} in highly vulnerable countries through research and dialogue. It recognises that such harm can go beyond what adaptation can reduce. But it makes no provision for liability or compensation. {{ref:nature-clim-074}} states that it gives no basis for either. Developed countries, particularly the United States, insisted on that no-liability clause.

nature-clim-026.title: Social vulnerability: harm shaped by society
nature-clim-026.text: Social vulnerability is the inability of people, organisations and societies to withstand harm from multiple stresses, such as social exclusion and natural hazards. It arises partly from social interactions, institutions and cultural values. At the individual level, marital status, employment and income all affect it. The lesson is that a catastrophe cannot be understood from the size of the shock alone. It also requires looking at people's assets and entitlements, what they own and what they can claim.

nature-clim-028.title: Biophysical and social vulnerability
nature-clim-028.text: Climate vulnerability splits into two main kinds. Biophysical vulnerability concerns the effects of physical hazards. Early studies focused on it, drawing on natural hazards research. Social vulnerability, described in {{ref:nature-clim-026}}, is shaped by political, economic and social structures. It is a people-centred view of why some are harmed more, driven by poverty, poor governance and conflict. Where the two meet, in a particular place, vulnerability peaks where sea level rise and changes in ecosystem services such as food access strike.

nature-clim-029.title: Climate vulnerability assessment: scoring who is at risk
nature-clim-029.text: To act on {{ref:nature-clim-027}}, decision-makers first need to measure it. Assessment tools range from global indices to local models and participatory methods. Global indices include the ND-GAIN Country Index, the INFORM Risk Index and the WorldRiskIndex. Such composite indices usually average a set of standardised indicators into one score. At a finer level, vulnerability curves link the size of a hazard, such as extreme heat or sea level rise, to the damage it causes.

nature-clim-033.title: Crop insurance: governments step in for farmers
nature-clim-033.text: Crop insurance is government-subsidised cover bought by farmers against crop losses from disasters such as hail, drought and floods, or against lost revenue. Governments stepped in because markets failed to give farmers tools to manage production risk. Hail is the exception. It is a narrow, local peril, so private firms insure it, while multi-peril cover is exposed to large-scale events. In the United States the federal government pays on average 62 percent of the premium, and about 90% of crop acreage is insured. India's National Agriculture Insurance Scheme insures whole areas instead of single farms, paying for yield shortfalls against the past five years.

nature-clim-035.title: Index-based insurance: paying out by rainfall, not by claim
nature-clim-035.text: Sending an assessor to every small farm after a drought costs more than the farms' policies are worth. For smallholders in developing countries, traditional indemnity insurance, which pays for each person's verified loss, is usually not viable. Index-based insurance offers a workaround. It pays out when an index closely tied to losses, such as rainfall or yield, crosses a set trigger. Paying by index avoids the cost of checking individual claims. It also sidesteps {{ref:nature-econ-004}}, because no one can manipulate the weather that triggers payment. Weather disasters hit many people at once, unlike thefts, which makes them hard to insure conventionally. Many indices now use satellite imagery. The results so far are modest. In developing countries it has needed subsidies to be viable, and uptake among smallholders remains low.

nature-clim-039.title: Flood insurance: protection that can encourage risk
nature-clim-039.text: Flood insurance covers losses from flooding and is one of the most widely used forms of {{ref:nature-clim-225}}. Rising sea levels, floods and windstorms threaten its affordability in exposed areas. It can also shape behavior. Critics say the subsidised US programme encouraged building and rebuilding in floodplains and on coasts. Its rules make flood-prone homes more likely to be rented cheaply to low-income, older or infirm people. That is an example of adverse selection, where the riskiest cases end up concentrated among those covered.

nature-clim-040.title: The base flood: the one-in-a-hundred-year benchmark
nature-clim-040.text: The base flood is a flood with a one percent chance of being equalled or exceeded in any year. It is also called the 100-year flood, and it is used to define floodplains. Its likelihood is worked out by statistical analysis of streamflow records. Urban growth increases runoff, so flood maps based on older data may understate the hazard.

nature-clim-036.title: Basis risk: when the index and the farm disagree
nature-clim-036.text: {{ref:nature-clim-035}} has a weak spot. Basis risk is the mismatch between what the index pays and the losses a particular farmer actually suffers. An index covers a whole area, and rainfall can differ from field to field. So some farmers lose their crops but get no payout, while others are paid without a loss. Because of this, farmers are reluctant to pay the same premiums as for standard insurance. Researchers aim to reduce basis risk with new data sources.
